Lastly, we reveal a discrepancy between LLMs' internal encoding and external behavior: they may encode the correct answer, yet consistently generate an incorrect one. Taken together, these insights deepen our understanding of LLM errors from the model's internal perspective, which can guide future research on enhancing error analysis and mitigation.

papers.title: LF-Steering: Latent Feature Activation Steering for Enhancing Semantic Consistency in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we precisely identify and modify latent feature representations to improve the semantic consistency of Large Language Models (LLMs) when responding to semantically equivalent paraphrased inputs?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes LF-Steering, a novel activation steering method that uses a sparse autoencoder (SAE) to decompose transformer layer hidden states into a sparsely activated, higher-dimensional feature space, enabling precise identification and adjustment of features responsible for semantic inconsistency to improve LLM performance.
papers.conclusion: The proposed LF-Steering method effectively enhances the semantic consistency of LLMs by enabling precise, feature-level activation steering, leading to significant task performance gains across a range of NLU and NLG datasets.
papers.key_findings:
LF-Steering achieves state-of-the-art performance in enhancing semantic consistency, outperforming baseline activation steering methods on NLU and NLG tasks.
Feature-level steering using SAE features significantly outperforms neuron-level (hidden state) steering, demonstrating the advantage of operating on decoupled feature representations.
The method shows good locality, not negatively impacting performance on out-of-domain datasets and sometimes improving it.
Middle to final transformer layers (layers 17-32 in LLama2-7B-Chat) are most significantly associated with semantic inconsistency.
The effectiveness of the method depends on selecting appropriate hyperparameters, such as the feature difference threshold and steering strength.
papers.limitation: Addressing semantic inconsistency at a single transformer layer may offer only a partial solution, as relevant latent representations may span multiple layers.
future_direction: Focus on identifying and steering circuits across multiple transformer layers to enhance the LLM's semantic consistency.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often generate inconsistent responses when prompted with semantically equivalent paraphrased inputs. Recently, activation steering, a technique that modulates LLMs' behaviours by adjusting their latent representations during inference time, has been explored to improve the semantic consistency of LLMs. However, these methods typically operate at the model component level, such as layer hidden states or attention head outputs. They face a challenge due to the ``polysemanticity issue'', where the model components of LLMs typically encode multiple entangled features, making precise steering difficult. To address this challenge, we drill down to feature-level representations and propose LF-Steering, a novel activation steering approach to precisely identify latent feature representations responsible for semantic inconsistency. More specifically, our method maps the hidden states of the relevant transformer layer into a sparsely activated, high-dimensional feature space based on a sparse autoencoder (SAE), ensuring model steering based on decoupled feature representations with minimal interference. Comprehensive experiments on NLU and NLG datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in enhancing semantic consistency, resulting in significant performance gains for various NLU and NLG tasks.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: How Pre-trained Language Models Capture Factual Knowledge? A Causal-Inspired Analysis
papers.research_question: How do pre-trained language models capture factual knowledge? Specifically, which word-level associations (knowledge-dependent, positionally close, highly co-occurred) do they depend on, and are these associations effective?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a causal-inspired analysis framework to quantify word-level dependence in PLMs for factual knowledge capture, and finds that PLMs rely more on positionally close and highly co-occurred associations than knowledge-dependent ones, which is ineffective for factual knowledge capture.
papers.conclusion: The analysis shows that PLMs rely more on ineffective associations (positionally close and highly co-occurred) and somewhat ignore effective knowledge-dependent clues, indicating that attention to knowledge-dependent association is needed for better factual knowledge capture.
papers.key_findings:
PLMs generate missing factual words more by positionally close and highly co-occurred words than by knowledge-dependent words.
The dependence on knowledge-dependent words is more effective for factual knowledge capture than dependence on positionally close and highly co-occurred words.
PLMs capture factual knowledge ineffectively because they depend more on inadequate associations.
papers.abstract: Recently, there has been a trend to investigate the factual knowledge captured by Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs). Many works show the PLMs' ability to fill in the missing factual words in cloze-style prompts such as "Dante was born in [MASK]." However, it is still a mystery how PLMs generate the results correctly: relying on effective clues or shortcut patterns? We try to answer this question by a causal-inspired analysis that quantitatively measures and evaluates the wordlevel patterns that PLMs depend on to generate the missing words. We check the words that have three typical associations with the missing words: knowledge-dependent, positionally close, and highly co-occurred. Our analysis shows: (1) PLMs generate the missing factual words more by the positionally close and highly co-occurred words than the knowledge-dependent words; (2) the dependence on the knowledge-dependent words is more effective than the positionally close and highly co-occurred words. Accordingly, we conclude that the PLMs capture the factual knowledge ineffectively because of depending on the inadequate associations.

papers.title: Bridging the Knowledge-Prediction Gap in LLMs on Multiple-Choice Questions
papers.research_question: What is the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs on multiple-choice questions and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a geometric interpretation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs and introduces KAPPA, an inference-time intervention that aligns knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream to mitigate the gap.
papers.conclusion: The knowledge-prediction gap is a pervasive phenomenon in LLMs, and representation-level alignment via methods like KAPPA can elicit more faithful predictions.
papers.key_findings:
The knowledge-prediction gap is widespread across diverse MCQ benchmarks and model families.
The gap can be geometrically interpreted as a misalignment between knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream.
KAPPA effectively reduces the gap and improves accuracy across benchmarks without additional training.
The gap is more pronounced in reasoning, truthfulness, and bias benchmarks compared to knowledge-intensive benchmarks.
The identified subspaces partially transfer across tasks requiring similar skills.
papers.limitation: The method relies on linearly accessible knowledge, leaving nonlinearly encoded knowledge unexplored.
future_direction: Developing more reliable methods to extract knowledge from model representations.
Understanding how nonlinearly encoded knowledge can be aligned.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on diverse tasks, their trustworthiness is limited by erratic behavior that is unfaithful to their internal knowledge. In particular, LLMs often fail on multiple-choice questions (MCQs) even if they encode correct answers in their hidden representations, revealing a misalignment between internal knowledge and output behavior. We investigate and mitigate this knowledge-prediction gap on MCQs through a three-step analysis of hidden representations. First, we quantify the prevalence and magnitude of the gap across models and datasets. Second, we provide a geometric interpretation by identifying distinct knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream. Third, we introduce KAPPA, a lightweight inference-time intervention that aligns the two subspaces within the residual stream to reduce the knowledge-prediction gap. Our results provide a geometric and interpretable explanation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs. Furthermore, KAPPA effectively reduces the gap across diverse MCQ benchmarks and models, and generalizes to free-form settings.

papers.title: Cognitive Dissonance: Why Do Language Model Outputs Disagree with Internal Representations of Truthfulness?
papers.research_question: Why do language model outputs disagree with internal representations of truthfulness, and is this due to deception or other factors like confabulation and heterogeneity?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that most disagreements between LM outputs and internal truthfulness representations are due to confabulation and heterogeneity, with deception being rare, and that probes are better calibrated than queries.
papers.conclusion: Disagreements between internal and external representations of truthfulness are predominantly due to different prediction pathways rather than latent deceptive intent, and the proposed taxonomy helps categorize these mismatches.
papers.key_findings:
Probes are consistently more accurate than direct queries on factual question-answering tasks.
Probes are substantially better calibrated than language model queries.
Most query-probe disagreements arise from confabulation (queries confident but probes uncertain) and heterogeneity (different performance on subsets), not deception.
Queries and probes are complementary, and ensembling them can improve accuracy over either alone.
The distribution of disagreement types varies across datasets, with deception being more prominent in CREAK.
papers.limitation:
Significant heterogeneity in the distribution of disagreement types across datasets, so findings may not generalize to future datasets.
Use of only a single prompt template for each experiment, which may not capture the full range of model behavior.
Only linear probes were used, and some information may be encoded non-linearly.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) can be used to evaluate the truth of factual statements in two ways: they can be either queried for statement probabilities, or probed for internal representations of truthfulness. Past work has found that these two procedures sometimes disagree, and that probes tend to be more accurate than LM outputs. This has led some researchers to conclude that LMs "lie" or otherwise encode non-cooperative communicative intents. Is this an accurate description of today's LMs, or can query-probe disagreement arise in other ways? We identify three different classes of disagreement, which we term confabulation, deception, and heterogeneity. In many cases, the superiority of probes is simply attributable to better calibration on uncertain answers rather than a greater fraction of correct, high-confidence answers. In some cases, queries and probes perform better on different subsets of inputs, and accuracy can further be improved by ensembling the two. Code is available at github.com/lingo-mit/lm-truthfulness.

papers.title: Benchmarking and Understanding Compositional Relational Reasoning of LLMs
papers.research_question: What is the capability of existing transformer large language models (LLMs) in solving compositional relational reasoning (CRR) tasks, and what are the underlying mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) benchmark for evaluating compositional relational reasoning in LLMs, revealing their deficiency, and discovers core circuits and True/False attention heads that are fundamental for CRR.
papers.conclusion: The GAR benchmark is challenging for mainstream LLMs and reveals a fundamental deficiency in compositional relational reasoning. Mechanistic interpretability analysis discovers reusable core circuits and identifies True/False attention heads that play fundamental roles in CRR across models and tasks.
papers.key_findings:
GAR is challenging for existing LLMs, with performance dropping significantly for harder tasks and the compositionality gap increasing with model scale.
Attribution patching reveals core circuits reused by Vicuna-33B across different GAR tasks, including a truthfulness sub-circuit and an in-context learning sub-circuit.
Intervention experiments show that correct functioning of identified vital attention heads (e.g., predicting, pre-predicting, higher-order local, induction, and relating heads) significantly impacts task performance.
Two classes of higher-order relating heads (True and False heads) are identified whose activations represent the abstract notion of true and false in GAR tasks.
The activation patterns of the True/False heads generalize to other datasets (SNLI and GoT), indicating they encode information for truthfulness classification beyond GAR.
papers.limitation: The circuit discovery is done manually without using automatic circuit discovery methods, which is left for future work.
future_direction: Automatic circuit discovery methods for larger models and more complex circuits.
papers.abstract: Compositional relational reasoning (CRR) is a hallmark of human intelligence, but we lack a clear understanding of whether and how existing transformer large language models (LLMs) can solve CRR tasks. To enable systematic exploration of the CRR capability of LLMs, we first propose a new synthetic benchmark called Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) by integrating and generalizing the essence of several tasks in mechanistic interpretability (MI) study in a unified framework. Evaluation shows that GAR is challenging enough for existing LLMs, revealing their fundamental deficiency in CRR. Meanwhile, it is easy enough for systematic MI study. Then, to understand how LLMs solve GAR tasks, we use attribution patching to discover the core circuits reused by Vicuna-33B across different tasks, and a set of vital attention heads. Intervention experiments show that the correct functioning of these heads significantly impacts task performance. Especially, we identify two classes of heads whose activations represent the abstract notion of true and false in GAR tasks respectively. They play fundamental roles in CRR across various models and tasks.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Enable Scalable and Reliable Circuit Identification in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently and robustly discover interpretable circuits in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method for circuit identification using discrete sparse autoencoders trained on attention head outputs, which is more efficient and robust than existing techniques.
papers.conclusion: Discrete sparse autoencoders offer a scalable, efficient, and robust approach for circuit identification in large language models, providing a promising direction for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The method outperforms or matches state-of-the-art circuit identification techniques (ACDC, HISP, SP) in precision and recall on three tasks (IOI, Greater-than, Docstring).
The method is robust to hyperparameter choices and requires only 5-10 text examples per task to learn robust representations.
The identified circuits can match or even outperform the full model's performance on the specific tasks with fewer components.
The method can identify negative components in circuits (e.g., negative name-mover heads in IOI) that other algorithms struggle to find.
The process is significantly faster, reducing runtime from hours to seconds compared to existing methods.
papers.limitation: The method currently only analyzes attention heads and not other components like MLP layers, which may be important for some circuits (e.g., Greater-than).
future_direction: Extending the method to analyze MLP layers and other model components.
Applying the method to larger models and more complex tasks.
Exploring the use of vector-quantized variational autoencoders (VQ-VAEs) as an alternative to sparse autoencoders.
papers.abstract: This paper introduces an efficient and robust method for discovering interpretable circuits in large language models using discrete sparse autoencoders. Our approach addresses key limitations of existing techniques, namely computational complexity and sensitivity to hyperparameters. We propose training sparse autoencoders on carefully designed positive and negative examples, where the model can only correctly predict the next token for the positive examples. We hypothesise that learned representations of attention head outputs will signal when a head is engaged in specific computations. By discretising the learned representations into integer codes and measuring the overlap between codes unique to positive examples for each head, we enable direct identification of attention heads involved in circuits without the need for expensive ablations or architectural modifications. On three well-studied tasks - indirect object identification, greater-than comparisons, and docstring completion - the proposed method achieves higher precision and recall in recovering ground-truth circuits compared to state-of-the-art baselines, while reducing runtime from hours to seconds. Notably, we require only 5-10 text examples for each task to learn robust representations. Our findings highlight the promise of discrete sparse autoencoders for scalable and efficient mechanistic interpretability, offering a new direction for analysing the inner workings of large language models.

papers.title: Language Models with Rationality
papers.research_question: How can we make model beliefs and their inferential relationships explicit and resolve inconsistencies so that answers are supported by interpretable chains of reasoning drawn from a consistent belief system?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REFLEX, a new system architecture that adds a rational layer on top of an LLM to construct explicit belief graphs and resolve inconsistencies, improving belief consistency without harming answer accuracy.
papers.conclusion: REFLEX is an important step towards improving confidence in system behavior and towards trustable deployment of LLMs in practical applications by providing interpretable reasoning and repairing latent inconsistencies.
papers.key_findings:
REFLEX significantly improves consistency (by 8%-11% absolute) without harming overall answer accuracy.
The rational layer provides faithful explanations by supporting answers with interpretable chains of reasoning from a consistent belief system.
The constraint reasoner can correct initially wrong answers, correct erroneous latent model beliefs, and identify and reject bad rules.
All three types of rules (p → h, XOR, MC) contribute to the system's consistency improvements.
Failure modes include missing rules, incorrect beliefs, incorrect rules, ambiguous statements, and multiple valid answers.
papers.limitation:
The reasoning component can make mistakes, resulting in the overall system rejecting true statements or accepting false ones.
The method is evaluated only on a T5-11B based LLM; effectiveness with newer and larger LLMs like ChatGPT and LLaMA remains to be evaluated.
No formal user study has been conducted to measure the value of belief graphs for providing explanations and gaining user trust.
future_direction: Incorporating the question's context in the belief statements to make semantics more precise and avoid ambiguity.
Using the belief graph to identify uncertain reasoning pieces and guide a human-in-the-loop mechanism for correction or validation.
Maintaining a persistent belief graph over multiple questions to make the system more consistent across questions in a dialog setting.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) are proficient at question-answering (QA), it is not always clear how (or even if) an answer follows from their latent "beliefs". This lack of interpretability is a growing impediment to widespread use of LLMs. To address this, our goals are to make model beliefs and their inferential relationships explicit, and to resolve inconsistencies that may exist, so that answers are supported by interpretable chains of reasoning drawn from a consistent network of beliefs. Our approach, which we call REFLEX, is to add a rational, self-reflecting layer on top of the LLM. First, given a question, we construct a belief graph using a backward-chaining process to materialize relevant model beliefs (including beliefs about answer candidates) and their inferential relationships. Second, we identify and minimize contradictions in that graph using a formal constraint reasoner. We find that REFLEX significantly improves consistency (by 8%-11% absolute) without harming overall answer accuracy, resulting in answers supported by faithful chains of reasoning drawn from a more consistent belief system. This suggests a new style of system architecture in which an LLM extended with a rational layer can provide an interpretable window into system beliefs, add a systematic reasoning capability, and repair latent inconsistencies present in the LLM.

papers.title: How Do Vision-Language Models Process Conflicting Information Across Modalities?
papers.research_question: How do vision-language models process conflicting information across modalities?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that vision-language models exhibit biases towards one modality when processing conflicting inputs, and identifies specific attention heads that can be intervened to improve performance and control the modality preference.
papers.conclusion: VLMs encounter difficulties with conflicting inputs, and their behavioral accuracy correlates with the representational salience of the target modality. Attention head interventions can manipulate the representational salience and improve performance.
papers.key_findings:
Models show performance degradation when presented with inconsistent image-caption pairs, and different models have different modality biases.
Internal representations encode unimodal information for both modalities and can detect consistency, but the target modality is not always more salient.
The representational salience of the target modality (measured by V-Measure) strongly correlates with behavioral accuracy.
The authors identify modality-agnostic router heads and modality-specific promotion heads through attention head interventions.
Intervening on these heads can improve performance and change representational salience across datasets.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on 7b-parameter multimodal large language models, which are only a subset of vision-language models.
future_direction: Extend findings to inputs from modalities beyond text and vision (e.g., audio, spatial).
Explore circuit analysis to understand interactions among attention heads and other components.
papers.abstract: AI models are increasingly required to be multimodal, integrating disparate input streams into a coherent state representation on which subsequent behaviors and actions can be based. This paper seeks to understand how such models behave when input streams present conflicting information. Focusing specifically on vision-language models, we provide inconsistent inputs (e.g., an image of a dog paired with the caption "A photo of a cat") and ask the model to report the information present in one of the specific modalities (e.g., "What does the caption say / What is in the image?"). We find that models often favor one modality over the other, e.g., reporting the image regardless of what the caption says, but that different models differ in which modality they favor. We find evidence that the behaviorally preferred modality is evident in the internal representational structure of the model, and that specific attention heads can restructure the representations to favor one modality over the other. Moreover, we find modality-agnostic "router heads" which appear to promote answers about the modality requested in the instruction, and which can be manipulated or transferred in order to improve performance across datasets and modalities. Together, the work provides essential steps towards identifying and controlling if and how models detect and resolve conflicting signals within complex multimodal environments.

papers.title: Fact Recall, Heuristics or Pure Guesswork? Precise Interpretations of Language Models for Fact Completion
papers.research_question: How do interpretability methods like causal tracing and information flow analysis differ across distinct prediction scenarios (exact fact recall, heuristics, guesswork, generic language modeling) in language models for fact completion?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PRISM, a method for constructing datasets to distinguish four prediction scenarios in fact completion, and shows that causal tracing and information flow analysis yield distinct patterns for each scenario, revealing different mechanisms for exact fact recall versus heuristics or guesswork.
papers.conclusion: The PRISM dataset and analyses provide a more nuanced understanding of fact completion in LMs, showing that interpretability methods must account for different prediction scenarios to avoid misleading conclusions.
papers.key_findings:
Exact fact recall shows a clear peak in averaged indirect effects at (last subject token, mid layer) MLP states, supporting previous conclusions about memory storage.
Guesswork and heuristics recall show a critical role of late last token position MLP sublayers, unlike exact fact recall.
Generic language modeling samples do not show the mid-layer MLP peak, indicating no memory access.
Combined samples of fact completion scenarios can misleadingly show the exact fact recall pattern, dominating other scenarios.
Information flow analysis reveals distinct patterns for each scenario, e.g., exact fact recall versus generic language modeling.
papers.limitation:
The approach is not intended to classify every instance into one of the four scenarios, but to produce high-quality examples of each one.
The samples and analysis are focused on the English language.
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) can make a correct prediction based on many possible signals in a prompt, not all corresponding to recall of factual associations. However, current interpretations of LMs fail to take this into account. For example, given the query "Astrid Lindgren was born in" with the corresponding completion "Sweden", no difference is made between whether the prediction was based on knowing where the author was born or assuming that a person with a Swedish-sounding name was born in Sweden. In this paper, we present a model-specific recipe - PrISM - for constructing datasets with examples of four different prediction scenarios: generic language modeling, guesswork, heuristics recall and exact fact recall. We apply two popular interpretability methods to the scenarios: causal tracing (CT) and information flow analysis. We find that both yield distinct results for each scenario. Results for exact fact recall and generic language modeling scenarios confirm previous conclusions about the importance of mid-range MLP sublayers for fact recall, while results for guesswork and heuristics indicate a critical role of late last token position MLP sublayers. In summary, we contribute resources for a more extensive and granular study of fact completion in LMs, together with analyses that provide a more nuanced understanding of how LMs process fact-related queries.

papers.title: On Memorization of Large Language Models in Logical Reasoning
papers.research_question: Does memorization explain LLMs' performance on reasoning benchmarks, and is memorization only detrimental to learning to reason?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a memorization score (LiMem) and a dynamic K&K benchmark to show that fine-tuned LLMs memorize training puzzles but also improve in generalization, developing reasoning skills alongside memorization.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that memorization and reasoning coexist in fine-tuned LLMs, and the proposed memorization score (LiMem) helps quantify the interplay between them.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can interpolate and memorize training puzzles after fine-tuning, achieving near-perfect accuracy, but struggle with slight variations.
Fine-tuning leads to heavy memorization but also consistently improves generalization performance on K&K puzzles.
LLMs develop reasoning skills on K&K puzzles alongside memorization, as shown by transferability across difficulty levels and probing internal representations.
Fine-tuning with detailed reasoning steps (CoT) can further boost generalization, even when fine-tuned with wrong reasoning steps.
Per-sample memorization score reveals how LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization when solving logical puzzles.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to Knights and Knaves puzzles and may not generalize to other reasoning tasks.
The memorization score LiMem may not capture all forms of memorization.
future_direction: Extend the study to other reasoning tasks beyond K&K puzzles.
Investigate the effect of model scale on memorization and reasoning.
Improve the memorization score to better capture memorization behaviors.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve good performance on challenging reasoning benchmarks, yet could also make basic reasoning mistakes. This contrasting behavior is puzzling when it comes to understanding the mechanisms behind LLMs' reasoning capabilities. One hypothesis is that the increasingly high and nearly saturated performance on common reasoning benchmarks could be due to the memorization of similar problems. In this paper, we systematically investigate this hypothesis with a quantitative measurement of memorization in reasoning tasks, using a dynamically generated logical reasoning benchmark based on Knights and Knaves (K&K) puzzles. We found that LLMs could interpolate the training puzzles (achieving near-perfect accuracy) after fine-tuning, yet fail when those puzzles are slightly perturbed, suggesting that the models heavily rely on memorization to solve those training puzzles. On the other hand, we show that while fine-tuning leads to heavy memorization, it also consistently improves generalization performance. In-depth analyses with perturbation tests, cross difficulty-level transferability, probing model internals, and fine-tuning with wrong answers suggest that the LLMs learn to reason on K&K puzzles despite training data memorization. This phenomenon indicates that LLMs exhibit a complex interplay between memorization and genuine reasoning abilities. Finally, our analysis with per-sample memorization score sheds light on how LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization in solving logical puzzles. Our code and data are available at https://memkklogic.github.io.

papers.title: Facts in Stats: Impacts of Pretraining Diversity on Language Model Generalization
papers.research_question: How does the diversity of pretraining data (in terms of contextual variation) impact the generalization of language models in learning both statistical patterns and factual associations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a synthetic testbed to study how pretraining diversity affects generalization, finding that diversity impacts in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance differently depending on contextual structure, and identifies optimization bottlenecks in embedding and unembedding layers.
papers.conclusion: Overall, the synthetic framework allows isolation of effects that would be confounded in large-scale studies, offering a controlled testbed for future investigations.
papers.key_findings:
Higher diversity can slow in-distribution factual recall while leaving in-distribution statistical accuracy largely unaffected.
Out-of-distribution effects depend on contextual structure: low diversity can severely impact factual recall, statistical accuracy, or both.
Data diversity introduces a cost-benefit dynamic: with limited training time, intermediate diversity levels are optimal.
The learning dynamics of the statistical and factual streams are coupled: increased complexity in one stream delays learning of both.
Through targeted interventions, optimization bottlenecks for out-of-distribution generalization are localized to the embedding and unembedding layers.
future_direction: Characterizing how context diversity and model capacity reshape the in-distribution loss landscape
papers.abstract: Language models are pretrained on sequences that blend statistical regularities (making text fluent) with factual associations between specific tokens (knowledge of facts). While recent work suggests that the variability of their interaction, such as paraphrases of factual associations, critically determines generalization ability, we lack a systematic analysis of these impacts. This paper introduces a flexible synthetic testbed that combines a statistical stream of generic tokens with an abstract factual stream of source-target token pairs, enabling fine-grained control over their interaction. The design enables the independent control of diversity nature by manipulating stream composition (contextual structure) and the diversity level by varying which statistical streams each fact appears in. Through controlled experiments, we find that while higher contextual diversity delays in-distribution (ID) factual accuracy, its impact on out-of-distribution (OOD) factual generalization depends critically on contextual structure. In some cases, OOD performance follows the same trend as ID, but in others, diversity becomes essential for non-trivial factual recall. Even when low diversity prohibits factual recall, optimal diversity levels depend on training duration. Beyond factual recall failures, we identify structures where statistical generalization fails independently, and others where both capabilities degrade. This shows how the interplay between contextual design and diversity level impacts different generalization aspects. Further, through a series of controlled interventions on the model components, we trace the OOD failures to distinct optimization bottlenecks, highlighting the importance of the embedding and unembedding layers. Our synthetic framework allows us to isolate effects that would be confounded in large-scale studies, offering a controlled testbed for future investigations.

papers.title: Exploiting Attention to Reveal Shortcomings in Memory Models
papers.research_question: How does attention analysis explain the contradictory performance of a memory network model on theory-of-mind question-answering tasks?
papers.core_contribution: By analyzing attention patterns, the paper explains why a memory network model fails on first-order belief questions but succeeds on second-order ones, linking success to task classification.
papers.conclusion: Attention analysis reveals shortcomings in memory models, and performance can be explained by how well the model classifies task types.
papers.key_findings:
The model is successful on second-order belief questions but not on first-order ones.
Attention patterns for second-order questions show sensitivity to task-relevant sentences like 'exited', aiding classification.
For first-order questions, attention is not sensitive to task type, leading to failures.
Equating success to task classification explains test-time failures and generalization.
With a modified dataset where answers are consistent, models succeed on first-order questions.
papers.abstract: The decision making processes of deep networks are difficult to understand and while their accuracy often improves with increased architectural complexity, so too does their opacity. Practical use of machine learning models, especially for question and answering applications, demands a system that is interpretable. We analyze the attention of a memory network model to reconcile contradictory performance on a challenging questionanswering dataset that is inspired by theoryof-mind experiments. We equate success on questions to task classification, which explains not only test-time failures but also how well the model generalizes to new training conditions.

papers.title: Explaining Self-Supervised Image Representations with Visual Probing
papers.research_question: How can we adapt NLP probing tasks to analyze self-supervised image representations, and what do these probes reveal about the semantic knowledge, complexity, and consistency encoded in such representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a visual probing framework that adapts NLP probing tasks to analyze self-supervised image representations, revealing insights about semantic knowledge, complexity, and consistency.
papers.conclusion: The visual probing framework is effective for understanding self-supervised image representations and provides complementary knowledge to linear evaluation. Relations between language and vision serve as an intuitive tool for explainable AI.
papers.key_findings:
Self-supervised representations contain strong semantic knowledge (as measured by the word content probing task).
The level of semantic knowledge does not correlate with target task accuracy.
Certain types of semantic knowledge (non-uniform textures) are represented better than others (uniform textures).
Self-supervised representations contain information about semantic complexity (sentence length and character bin tasks).
Self-supervised representations struggle to retain information about semantic consistency (SOMO task).
papers.abstract: Recently introduced self-supervised methods for image representation learning provide on par or superior results to their fully supervised competitors, yet the corresponding efforts to explain the self-supervised approaches lag behind. Motivated by this observation, we introduce a novel visual probing framework for explaining the self-supervised models by leveraging probing tasks employed previously in natural language processing. The probing tasks require knowledge about semantic relationships between image parts. Hence, we propose a systematic approach to obtain analogs of natural language in vision, such as visual words, context, and taxonomy. We show the effectiveness and applicability of those analogs in the context of explaining self-supervised representations. Our key findings emphasize that relations between language and vision can serve as an effective yet intuitive tool for discovering how machine learning models work, independently of data modality. Our work opens a plethora of research pathways towards more explainable and transparent AI.

papers.title: Knowledge Neurons in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge stored in pretrained Transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of knowledge neurons and a gradient-based attribution method to identify them in pretrained Transformers, demonstrating their role in storing factual knowledge and enabling model editing.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that factual knowledge in pretrained Transformers is stored in specific neurons (knowledge neurons) within feed-forward networks, and these neurons can be identified and manipulated to edit knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge neurons identified by the proposed attribution method are positively correlated with the expression of specific factual knowledge.
Suppressing or amplifying the activation of identified knowledge neurons significantly decreases or increases the probability of the correct answer, respectively.
Knowledge neurons are more activated by prompts expressing their corresponding fact than by control prompts.
Knowledge neurons can be used to update or erase specific factual knowledge in the model with minimal impact on other knowledge.
papers.limitation:
Examines knowledge neurons based on the fill-in-the-blank cloze task, while knowledge can be expressed in more implicit ways.
Interactions between knowledge neurons remain underexplored.
Focuses on factual knowledge for ease of evaluation, though the method is applicable to other knowledge types.
Uses single-word blanks in cloze queries, requiring extension to multi-word answers.
future_direction: Investigate whether Transformers can utilize stored knowledge in a generalized way, such as for reasoning.
Explore interactions between knowledge neurons.
Extend the method to other types of knowledge beyond factual knowledge.
Extend to multi-word blanks in cloze queries.
Investigate knowledge neurons in multilingual pretrained Transformers.
papers.abstract: Large-scale pretrained language models are surprisingly good at recalling factual knowledge presented in the training corpus. In this paper, we present preliminary studies on how factual knowledge is stored in pretrained Transformers by introducing the concept of knowledge neurons. Specifically, we examine the fill-in-the-blank cloze task for BERT. Given a relational fact, we propose a knowledge attribution method to identify the neurons that express the fact. We find that the activation of such knowledge neurons is positively correlated to the expression of their corresponding facts. In our case studies, we attempt to leverage knowledge neurons to edit (such as update, and erase) specific factual knowledge without fine-tuning. Our results shed light on understanding the storage of knowledge within pretrained Transformers. The code is available at https://github.com/Hunter-DDM/knowledge-neurons.

papers.title: Non-Linear Inference Time Intervention: Improving LLM Truthfulness
papers.research_question: How can LLM truthfulness be improved by enhancing inference-time intervention with non-linear probing and multi-token context?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Non-Linear ITI (NL-ITI), which enhances the Inference Time Intervention framework by using non-linear probing and multi-token context to better identify and bias attention heads towards truthfulness, improving performance on truthfulness benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: NL-ITI significantly improves LLM truthfulness by enhancing probing and intervention methods, demonstrating the potential of inference-time representation editing for safer and more accurate AI.
papers.key_findings:
NL-ITI achieves over 16% relative improvement in MC1 on TruthfulQA compared to ITI.
NL-ITI shows better generalization on benchmarks like ARC, MMLU, and OpenBookQA with slightly higher cross-entropy.
Non-linear probing with MLP improves the accuracy of identifying truthful attention heads compared to linear probing.
Using multiple tokens for probing and intervention enhances performance, with optimal results at 6 tokens for intervention and 4 for probing.
Truthful knowledge is distributed across multiple tokens, not just the last token.
papers.limitation: The need for labeled data is a limiting factor of NL-ITI approach.
future_direction: Explore use of unsupervised models.
papers.abstract: In this work, we explore LLM's internal representation space to identify attention heads that contain the most truthful and accurate information. We further developed the Inference Time Intervention (ITI) framework, which lets bias LLM without the need for fine-tuning. The improvement manifests in introducing a non-linear multi-token probing and multi-token intervention: Non-Linear ITI (NL-ITI), which significantly enhances performance on evaluation benchmarks. NL-ITI is tested on diverse multiple-choice datasets, including TruthfulQA, on which we report over 16% relative MC1 (accuracy of model pointing to the correct answer) improvement with respect to the baseline ITI results. Moreover, we achieved a 10% relative improvement over the recently released Truth Forest (TrFf) method that also focused on ITI improvement.

papers.title: A Theoretical Understanding of Self-Correction through In-context Alignment
papers.research_question: How does the self-correction capability arise in large language models (LLMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a theoretical analysis showing that transformers can perform self-correction via in-context alignment, and proposes the Checking as Context (CaC) method which applies this insight to alleviate social bias and defend against jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: Self-correction in LLMs can be understood as a form of in-context alignment, and transformers possess the inherent architectural capability to perform it, which has practical implications for improving model safety and reducing bias.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can implement gradient descent for common alignment objectives (Bradley-Terry, Plackett-Luce) in-context, providing a mechanism for self-correction.
The quality of the reward signal (critic) is crucial for effective self-correction.
Realistic transformer components (softmax attention, multi-head attention, FFN, stacked layers) are necessary for implementing the ranking and refinement operations required for in-context alignment.
The proposed Checking as Context (CaC) method, based on the theoretical insights, can effectively reduce social bias in model outputs.
CaC can significantly reduce the success rate of various jailbreak attacks without external feedback.
papers.limitation: The theoretical analysis only considers a simplified self-correction pipeline; in practice, prompt design has a large effect on performance.
future_direction: Further research on understanding, exploiting, and enhancing self-correction for building better foundation models.
Investigating the effect of prompt design on self-correction performance.
papers.abstract: Going beyond mimicking limited human experiences, recent studies show initial evidence that, like humans, large language models (LLMs) are capable of improving their abilities purely by self-correction, i.e., correcting previous responses through self-examination, in certain circumstances. Nevertheless, little is known about how such capabilities arise. In this work, based on a simplified setup akin to an alignment task, we theoretically analyze self-correction from an in-context learning perspective, showing that when LLMs give relatively accurate self-examinations as rewards, they are capable of refining responses in an in-context way. Notably, going beyond previous theories on over-simplified linear transformers, our theoretical construction underpins the roles of several key designs of realistic transformers for self-correction: softmax attention, multi-head attention, and the MLP block. We validate these findings extensively on synthetic datasets. Inspired by these findings, we also illustrate novel applications of self-correction, such as defending against LLM jailbreaks, where a simple self-correction step does make a large difference. We believe that these findings will inspire further research on understanding, exploiting, and enhancing self-correction for building better foundation models.

papers.title: Meaningless Tokens, Meaningful Gains: How Activation Shifts Enhance LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: Why does inserting meaningless tokens improve LLM reasoning performance, and how can this effect be harnessed?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic explanation for how meaningless tokens improve LLM reasoning via activation redistribution and introduces ARM, a lightweight inference-time method that reproduces this effect.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that activation redistribution is a key mechanism behind the meaningless-token effect and that ARM effectively harnesses this mechanism to improve LLM reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Inserting meaningless tokens induces an affine transformation on attention outputs, leading to activation redistribution in MLP layers.
Activation redistribution reduces near-zero activations and increases variance, enhancing the model's representational capacity for reasoning.
The proposed ARM method adaptively shifts near-zero activations outward, improving reasoning performance without changing input tokens.
ARM consistently improves performance across diverse models and reasoning benchmarks while being simple to implement.
papers.limitation:
Our method is primarily evaluated on reasoning tasks; its effectiveness on non-reasoning tasks is limited.
The hyperparameters of ARM need to be tuned per model family.
future_direction: Extending ARM to more layers or combining it with other inference-time optimizations.
Exploring the effect on non-reasoning tasks and automatic hyperparameter tuning.
papers.abstract: Motivated by the puzzling observation that inserting long sequences of meaningless tokens before the query prompt can consistently enhance LLM reasoning performance, this work analyzes the underlying mechanism driving this phenomenon and based on these insights proposes a more principled method that allows for similar performance gains. First, we find that the improvements arise from a redistribution of activations in the LLM's MLP layers, where near zero activations become less frequent while large magnitude activations increase. This redistribution enhances the model's representational capacity by suppressing weak signals and promoting stronger, more informative ones. Building on this insight, we propose the Activation Redistribution Module (ARM), a lightweight inference-time technique that modifies activations directly without altering the input sequence. ARM adaptively identifies near-zero activations after the non-linear function and shifts them outward, implicitly reproducing the beneficial effects of meaningless tokens in a controlled manner. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks and model architectures clearly show that ARM consistently improves LLM performance on reasoning tasks while requiring only a few lines of simple code to implement. Our findings deliver both a clear mechanistic explanation for the unexpected benefits of meaningless tokens and a simple yet effective technique that harnesses activation redistribution to further improve LLM performance.

papers.title: On the Entity-Level Alignment in Crosslingual Consistency
papers.research_question: What factors give rise to crosslingual consistency in multilingual LLMs, and do failures in entity alignment cause inconsistencies?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides the first systematic analysis linking crosslingual consistency to entity-level alignment, introduces two prompting methods (SUBSUB and SUBINJ) that improve factual recall and consistency, and uses mechanistic interpretability to show these methods enhance entity representation alignment through pivot-language processing.
papers.conclusion: Entity alignment is a key factor underlying crosslingual consistency in multilingual LLMs, and the proposed prompting methods offer effective and practical strategies for improving multilingual factual prediction by enhancing this alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Crosslingual consistency is strongly correlated with entity alignment across all studied models.
Consistent factual recall rarely occurs without correctly aligning either the subject or object entities between two languages.
The proposed prompting methods SUBSUB and SUBINJ, which incorporate English translations of subjects, substantially improve factual recall accuracy and consistency, especially in English-centric models.
Mechanistic analysis using Logit Lens shows that SUBSUB and SUBINJ interventions reinforce entity representation alignment in the model's internal conceptual space.
The model's conceptual space is biased towards high-resource languages like English, explaining why using English subject translations is more effective than using other languages.
papers.limitation: Inconsistency can also stem from failure in the processing stage – i.e., the model lacks the factual knowledge so it cannot retrieve the correct object in the conceptual space, which is beyond the scope of this paper.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (LLMs) are expected to recall factual knowledge consistently across languages. However, the factors that give rise to such crosslingual consistency -- and its frequent failure -- remain poorly understood. In this work, we hypothesize that these inconsistencies may arise from failures in entity alignment, the process of mapping subject and object entities into a shared conceptual space across languages. To test this, we assess alignment through entity-level (subject and object) translation tasks, and find that consistency is strongly correlated with alignment across all studied models, with misalignment of subjects or objects frequently resulting in inconsistencies. Building on this insight, we propose SubSub and SubInj, two effective methods that integrate English translations of subjects into prompts across languages, leading to substantial gains in both factual recall accuracy and consistency. Finally, our mechanistic analysis reveals that these interventions reinforce the entity representation alignment in the conceptual space through model's internal pivot-language processing, offering effective and practical strategies for improving multilingual factual prediction.

papers.title: Discovering Latent Knowledge in Language Models Without Supervision
papers.research_question: How can we discover latent knowledge in language models without supervision by finding consistent directions in activation space?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Contrast-Consistent Search (CCS), an unsupervised method to find latent knowledge in language model activations by enforcing logical consistency properties.
papers.conclusion: The work provides an initial step towards discovering what language models know independently of what they say, without requiring ground truth labels.
papers.key_findings:
CCS outperforms zero-shot accuracy by 4% on average across models and datasets.
CCS is robust to misleading prompts, maintaining high accuracy even when models are prompted to generate incorrect answers.
CCS finds a task-agnostic representation of truth that transfers well across different datasets.
CCS does not merely recover model outputs and can leverage intermediate layers more effectively.
Truth is a salient feature in model representations, often identifiable with simple methods like top principal component.
papers.abstract: Existing techniques for training language models can be misaligned with the truth: if we train models with imitation learning, they may reproduce errors that humans make; if we train them to generate text that humans rate highly, they may output errors that human evaluators can't detect. We propose circumventing this issue by directly finding latent knowledge inside the internal activations of a language model in a purely unsupervised way. Specifically, we introduce a method for accurately answering yes-no questions given only unlabeled model activations. It works by finding a direction in activation space that satisfies logical consistency properties, such as that a statement and its negation have opposite truth values. We show that despite using no supervision and no model outputs, our method can recover diverse knowledge represented in large language models: across 6 models and 10 question-answering datasets, it outperforms zero-shot accuracy by 4\% on average. We also find that it cuts prompt sensitivity in half and continues to maintain high accuracy even when models are prompted to generate incorrect answers. Our results provide an initial step toward discovering what language models know, distinct from what they say, even when we don't have access to explicit ground truth labels.

papers.title: Too Big to Fool: Resisting Deception in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do language models of varying capacities within the same family balance in-context information against their internal world models, particularly when faced with intentionally misleading prompts?
papers.core_contribution: Larger language models exhibit greater resilience to deceptive prompts, demonstrating an advanced ability to integrate conflicting in-context information with their internal knowledge, without simply ignoring prompts or relying on memorization.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces an evaluation strategy that re-uses existing benchmarks with minimal changes to study LLM behavior. Experiments show that larger models are more resilient to deceptive prompts, indicating a better ability to integrate prompt information with internal knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models consistently show a smaller Relative Accuracy Drop when given deceptive hints, indicating higher resilience to misinformation.
Larger models do not ignore in-context information; they effectively follow legitimate instructions and utilize truthful hints.
The resilience is not due to memorization, as shown by control experiments with overfitted models and a model without prior exposure to the test data.
Larger models generally exhibit better instruction-following capabilities, except for the Gemma family which is an outlier.
Models can infer missing information from answer choices, maintaining accuracy above chance even when the question is removed.
papers.limitation:
The study focused exclusively on multiple-choice datasets, which may not capture nuances of open-ended or generative tasks.
Experiments involved only open-source LLMs, limiting generalizability to proprietary models with different architectures or training.
papers.abstract: Large language models must balance their weight-encoded knowledge with in-context information from prompts to generate accurate responses. This paper investigates this interplay by analyzing how models of varying capacities within the same family handle intentionally misleading in-context information. Our experiments demonstrate that larger models exhibit higher resilience to deceptive prompts, showcasing an advanced ability to interpret and integrate prompt information with their internal knowledge. Furthermore, we find that larger models outperform smaller ones in following legitimate instructions, indicating that their resilience is not due to disregarding in-context information. We also show that this phenomenon is likely not a result of memorization but stems from the models' ability to better leverage implicit task-relevant information from the prompt alongside their internally stored knowledge.

papers.title: Position: Mechanistic Interpretability Should Prioritize Feature Consistency in SAEs
papers.research_question: How can feature consistency in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be achieved and measured to improve the reliability of mechanistic interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: This position paper argues that mechanistic interpretability should prioritize feature consistency in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and proposes the Pairwise Dictionary Mean Correlation Coefficient (PW-MCC) as a practical metric to measure consistency. It shows that high consistency is achievable with appropriate architectural choices (e.g., TopK SAEs) and that high PW-MCC correlates with semantic similarity of feature explanations.
papers.conclusion: The paper calls for a community-wide shift towards valuing and systematically measuring feature consistency in SAEs for cumulative progress in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
High feature consistency (PW-MCC ≈ 0.80) is achievable with TopK SAEs on real-world LLM activations.
PW-MCC reliably tracks ground-truth feature recovery (GT-MCC) in synthetic experiments.
Feature consistency is frequency-dependent: more frequent features are learned more consistently.
Different SAE architectures yield different levels of consistency, with TopK SAEs performing best.
High PW-MCC scores correlate strongly with the semantic similarity of feature explanations.
papers.limitation:
The focus is on SAEs, and other interpretability methods may have different consistency challenges.
The study uses a specific metric (PW-MCC) for a specific notion of consistency (strong feature consistency).
The real-world experiments are limited to two base models and one dataset.
The automated interpretation pipeline has its own limitations.
future_direction: Extending consistency analysis to other interpretability methods beyond SAEs.
Developing more nuanced metrics for consistency that go beyond strong feature consistency.
Investigating the relationship between consistency and downstream task performance.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are a prominent tool in mechanistic interpretability (MI) for decomposing neural network activations into interpretable features. However, the aspiration to identify a canonical set of features is challenged by the observed inconsistency of learned SAE features across different training runs, undermining the reliability and efficiency of MI research. This position paper argues that mechanistic interpretability should prioritize feature consistency in SAEs -- the reliable convergence to equivalent feature sets across independent runs. We propose using the Pairwise Dictionary Mean Correlation Coefficient (PW-MCC) as a practical metric to operationalize consistency and demonstrate that high levels are achievable (0.80 for TopK SAEs on LLM activations) with appropriate architectural choices. Our contributions include detailing the benefits of prioritizing consistency; providing theoretical grounding and synthetic validation using a model organism, which verifies PW-MCC as a reliable proxy for ground-truth recovery; and extending these findings to real-world LLM data, where high feature consistency strongly correlates with the semantic similarity of learned feature explanations. We call for a community-wide shift towards systematically measuring feature consistency to foster robust cumulative progress in MI.

papers.title: LLM Factoscope: Uncovering LLMs' Factual Discernment through Inner States Analysis
papers.research_question: Can we leverage the inner states of LLMs for factual detection without external resources?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LLM Factoscope, a pipeline that leverages inner states of LLMs for factual detection, achieving over 96% accuracy on a custom dataset.
papers.conclusion: The paper discovers effective inner states for factual detection and introduces LLM Factoscope, a pipeline that leverages these inner states to detect the factuality of LLM outputs, achieving high accuracy on custom datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Distinguishable patterns exist in LLMs' inner states when generating factual versus non-factual content.
LLM Factoscope achieves over 96% accuracy in factual detection across various LLM architectures.
The model generalizes to some extent but performance varies across different relations and models.
Each sub-model (processing different inner states) contributes to the overall performance and generalization capability.
The most influential features for factual detection are located in the middle to later layers of the LLMs.
papers.limitation:
Assumes LLMs' training corpora are predominantly factual, despite potential inclusion of non-factual content.
The custom dataset may not fully represent the diversity and complexity of real-world knowledge.
Generalization may be challenged when data types significantly deviate from those in the training dataset.
future_direction: Fine-tuning the model with new, more representative datasets to refine accuracy and broaden applicability.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized various domains with extensive knowledge and creative capabilities. However, a critical issue with LLMs is their tendency to produce outputs that diverge from factual reality. This phenomenon is particularly concerning in sensitive applications such as medical consultation and legal advice, where accuracy is paramount. In this paper, we introduce the LLM factoscope, a novel Siamese network-based model that leverages the inner states of LLMs for factual detection. Our investigation reveals distinguishable patterns in LLMs' inner states when generating factual versus non-factual content. We demonstrate the LLM factoscope's effectiveness across various architectures, achieving over 96% accuracy in factual detection. Our work opens a new avenue for utilizing LLMs' inner states for factual detection and encourages further exploration into LLMs' inner workings for enhanced reliability and transparency.

papers.title: On Relation-Specific Neurons in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do relation-specific neurons exist in large language models, i.e., neurons that focus on a relation itself independent of any entity, and what are their properties?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates the existence of relation-specific neurons in LLMs and provides evidence for their properties: cumulativity, versatility, and interference.
papers.conclusion: Relation-specific neurons exist in LLMs and exhibit properties of cumulativity, versatility, and interference, indicating distributed and overlapping encoding of relational knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Relation-specific neurons exist in LLMs and are located primarily in the middle layers.
Neuron cumulativity: Multiple neurons jointly contribute to processing facts involving a relation, with no single neuron fully encoding a fact.
Neuron versatility: Neurons can be shared across multiple closely related as well as less related relations, and some transfer across languages.
Neuron interference: Deactivating neurons specific to one relation can improve LLMs' factual recall performance for facts of other relations.
The effect of deactivating relation-specific neurons is more pronounced when more neurons are deactivated, and the neurons are effective across different prompt templates and languages.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to a set of 12 relations and two model families (LLama-2 and Gemma).
future_direction: Extend analysis to more relations and model families.
Investigate the dynamics of relation-specific neurons during training.
Explore whether similar neurons exist for other types of knowledge or tasks.
papers.abstract: In large language models (LLMs), certain \emph{neurons} can store distinct pieces of knowledge learned during pretraining. While factual knowledge typically appears as a combination of \emph{relations} and \emph{entities}, it remains unclear whether some neurons focus on a relation itself -- independent of any entity. We hypothesize such neurons \emph{detect} a relation in the input text and \emph{guide} generation involving such a relation. To investigate this, we study the LLama-2 family on a chosen set of relations, with a \textit{statistics}-based method. Our experiments demonstrate the existence of relation-specific neurons. We measure the effect of selectively deactivating candidate neurons specific to relation $r$ on the LLM's ability to handle (1) facts involving relation $r$ and (2) facts involving a different relation $r' \neq r$. With respect to their capacity for encoding relation information, we give evidence for the following three properties of relation-specific neurons. \textbf{(i) Neuron cumulativity.} Multiple neurons jointly contribute to processing facts involving relation $r$, with no single neuron fully encoding a fact in $r$ on its own. \textbf{(ii) Neuron versatility.} Neurons can be shared across multiple closely related as well as less related relations. In addition, some relation neurons transfer across languages. \textbf{(iii) Neuron interference.} Deactivating neurons specific to one relation can improve LLMs' factual recall performance for facts of other relations. We make our code and data publicly available at https://github.com/cisnlp/relation-specific-neurons.

papers.title: Generalization or Memorization: Dynamic Decoding for Mode Steering
papers.research_question: How can we understand, identify, and control the distinct reasoning modes (generalization vs. memorization) in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Dynamic Mode Steering (DMS), a training-free inference-time algorithm that uses a linear probe and activation steering to dynamically steer LLMs from memorization to generalization, improving performance on reasoning and faithfulness tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a theoretical framework based on the Information Bottleneck to explain generalization and memorization, and introduces DMS, an inference-time control method that improves reasoning and factual accuracy by steering models towards generalization circuits.
papers.key_findings:
DMS significantly improves logical reasoning performance on GSM8K and commonsense reasoning on HellaSwag.
DMS reduces the generation of memorized falsehoods, improving factual accuracy on TruthfulQA.
The optimal intervention layer for DMS is identified via causal tracing, and performance degrades if applied at non-optimal layers.
The steering strength hyperparameter α has a concave relationship with performance, indicating a trade-off.
DMS outperforms strong baselines like greedy decoding, nucleus sampling, and contrastive decoding.
papers.limitation: Standard probing only reveals correlations and may detect features not causally used by the model.
future_direction: Development of unsupervised methods for discovering behavior vectors.
Extending DMS to multi-attribute control.
Further theoretical work to deepen the connection between the Information Bottleneck principle and the geometry of activation space.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit a troubling duality, capable of both remarkable generalization and brittle, verbatim memorization of their training data. This unpredictability undermines their reliability in high-stakes applications. In this work, we propose a unified framework to understand, identify, and control these distinct reasoning modes. First, we introduce a theoretical model based on the Information Bottleneck (IB) principle, formalizing generalization as the learning of a compressed, task-relevant representation and memorization as a failure to compress. Building on this theory, we develop Dynamic Mode Steering (DMS), a novel inference-time algorithm which comprises two components: (1) a lightweight, causally-grounded linear probe that identifies the model's instantaneous reliance on memorization, and (2) a dynamic activation steering mechanism that nudges the model's computation towards pre-identified generalization circuits. We frame DMS as a form of adaptive, self-contrastive decoding. Experiments on reasoning and faithfulness tasks demonstrate that DMS significantly improves logical consistency and factual accuracy, thereby offering a principled approach to enhancing LLM reliability.

papers.title: On the Generalizability of "Competition of Mechanisms: Tracing How Language Models Handle Facts and Counterfactuals"
papers.research_question: Does the competition of mechanisms between factual recall and counterfactual repetition, as identified by Ortu et al. (2024), generalize to larger models, different prompt structures, and across domains?
papers.core_contribution: The attention head ablation method from Ortu et al. (2024) does not generalize well; its effectiveness varies significantly with model architecture, prompt structure, and domain.
papers.conclusion: The competition of mechanisms identified by Ortu et al. (2024) is not fully generalizable; experimental findings in mechanistic interpretability are highly dependent on the specific model, prompt structure, and domain.
papers.key_findings:
Successfully reproduced the original findings on GPT-2 small and Pythia 6.9B regarding positional information encoding, attention block dominance, and attention head specialization.
In Llama 3.1 8B, attention head specialization is greatly reduced, and the logit lens method shows limited early-layer activity and a sharp final-layer activation.
Changing the prompt structure to a question-answering format reduces the model's propensity to repeat the counterfactual, indicating sensitivity to repetition.
The choice of premise word (e.g., 'Redefine', 'Validate') affects the rate of factual vs. counterfactual predictions and the effectiveness of attention head ablation.
The effectiveness of the proposed attention head ablation varies across domains; it works best for domains where the factual token is leaked in the subject (e.g., 'Autos and Vehicles') and fails for others.
papers.limitation:
The logit lens method may be unreliable for larger models like Llama 3.1 8B, potentially failing to capture early-layer mechanisms.
The filtered MQuAKE dataset used for domain analysis is very small (228 prompts), limiting definitive conclusions.
Most extended findings rely on GPT-2 small and a dataset derived from Ortu et al. (2024), limiting generalizability to other models and datasets.
future_direction: Investigate whether larger models distribute work more evenly across heads or if newer interpretability techniques (e.g., circuit analysis, tuned lens) are needed to capture their mechanisms.
Conduct a deeper analysis of why certain dataset domains impact attention head activation, distinguishing between token leakage, topic words, and task difficulty.
Extend the findings to different, larger datasets and models, as well as new prompt structures and premise words.
papers.abstract: We present a reproduction study of "Competition of Mechanisms: Tracing How Language Models Handle Facts and Counterfactuals" (Ortu et al., 2024), which investigates competition of mechanisms in language models between factual recall and counterfactual in-context repetition. Our study successfully reproduces their primary findings regarding the localization of factual and counterfactual information, the dominance of attention blocks in mechanism competition, and the specialization of attention heads in handling competing information. We reproduce their results on both GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019) and Pythia 6.9B (Biderman et al., 2023). We extend their work in three significant directions. First, we explore the generalizability of these findings to even larger models by replicating the experiments on Llama 3.1 8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024), discovering greatly reduced attention head specialization. Second, we investigate the impact of prompt structure by introducing variations where we avoid repeating the counterfactual statement verbatim or we change the premise word, observing a marked decrease in the logit for the counterfactual token. Finally, we test the validity of the authors' claims for prompts of specific domains, discovering that certain categories of prompts skew the results by providing the factual prediction token as part of the subject of the sentence. Overall, we find that the attention head ablation proposed in Ortu et al. (2024) is ineffective for domains that are underrepresented in their dataset, and that the effectiveness varies based on model architecture, prompt structure, domain and task.

papers.title: Diagnosing Knowledge Conflict in Multimodal Long-Chain Reasoning
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) in long chain-of-thought reasoning often fail when different knowledge sources provide conflicting signals. We formalize these failures under a unified notion of knowledge conflict, distinguishing input-level objective conflict from process-level effective conflict. Through probing internal representations, we reveal that: (I) Linear Separability: different conflict types are explicitly encoded as linearly separable features rather than entangled; (II) Depth Localization: conflict signals concentrate in mid-to-late layers, indicating a distinct processing stage for conflict encoding; (III) Hierarchical Consistency: aggregating noisy token-level signals along trajectories robustly recovers input-level conflict types; and (IV) Directional Asymmetry: reinforcing the model's implicit source preference under conflict is far easier than enforcing the opposite source. Our findings provide a mechanism-level view of multimodal reasoning under knowledge conflict and enable principled diagnosis and control of long-CoT failures.

papers.title: Editing Conceptual Knowledge for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs possess the capability to modify concepts (conceptual knowledge) and how to evaluate such modifications.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the task of conceptual knowledge editing for LLMs, constructs a benchmark dataset ConceptEdit, and establishes a suite of evaluation metrics including Instance Change and Concept Consistency.
